direct_answer: Intermediate care is short-term support to help you recover, stay independent and avoid unnecessary hospital admission. It can be at home, in a community bed or a care home. It is often free for up to six weeks in England. Arrangements differ in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

content:
After illness or a hospital stay, you may need extra support for a while.

This guide explains intermediate care. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Types of intermediate care

  • Reablement at home.
  • Rehabilitation in a community bed.
  • Crisis response to avoid admission.

Costs

In England, intermediate care is usually free for up to six weeks. Ask locally elsewhere in the UK.

Making the most of it

  • Set clear goals.
  • Practise exercises between visits.
  • Tell staff about your arthritis.

When it ends

Ask about ongoing support and a needs assessment if you need longer-term care.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Who arranges it?

Hospital or community teams.

Can I ask for it?

Ask your GP or discharge team.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Care after a hospital stay
  • NICE NG74: Intermediate care including reablement
  • NICE NG27: Transition between inpatient hospital settings and community or care home settings

Educational information for people in the United Kingdom — not a diagnosis or personal medical advice. Charity no. 1218461. Reviewed by Louis Maxwell (HCPC PH128483). Living With Arthritis is an independent charity and is not part of Arthritis UK (formerly Versus Arthritis). Everyone's situation is different, so follow the advice of your own GP and care team. If you feel very unwell, call 999 or go to A&E. For urgent advice, contact NHS 111 (NHS 24 on 111 in Scotland; in Northern Ireland, your GP or GP out-of-hours service).
